questions.q: Who is the author of "The Rocking-horse Winner," and what two contrasting social backgrounds did his parents come from?
questions.a: The author is D.H. Lawrence. His father was a coal miner (working class) and his mother was a former schoolmistress from a genteel, middle-class background. A wrong answer (e.g., naming a different author or vague "poor/rich") reveals the student has not read the "About the Author" box or cannot extract the specific class contrast that drives the story’s central marriage dynamic.

questions.q: In your own words, explain how the phrase "turned to dust" in the glossary connects to the mother’s experience of marriage as described in the opening paragraph.
questions.a: "Turned to dust" metaphorically captures how the mother’s romantic expectations ("married for love") disintegrated into barren reality ("love turned to dust"), leaving emotional emptiness rather than fulfilment. A wrong answer that treats "dust" only as literal dirt misses the modernist use of metaphor to convey psychological erosion, indicating the student reads literally rather than symbolically.

questions.q: Using the glossary words "careered," "overwrought," and "brazening it out," predict the psychological state of the protagonist Paul during his rocking-horse rides and his relationship with the adults around him.
questions.a: "Careered" suggests uncontrolled, frantic motion; "overwrought" indicates extreme nervous tension; "brazening it out" implies Paul forces a false confidence to hide his secret from adults. Together they predict a boy driven to manic, desperate rituals he must conceal. A wrong answer listing definitions without synthesising them into a character portrait shows inability to apply lexical clues to narrative prediction.

questions.q: Analyse how the historical context of post-WWI England (inflation, shattered aristocracy, rise of consumer credit) shapes the story’s personification of the house whispering "There must be more money."
questions.a: The whisper externalises the pervasive, unspoken middle-class terror of downward mobility in the 1920s: the house becomes a surrogate for a society where maintaining appearances requires ever-increasing debt. A wrong answer that treats the whisper as merely a supernatural element or a simple plot device fails to connect the literary personification to its historical referent, missing the modernist critique of capitalism.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "Knowing Lawrence’s biography is essential to understanding the story; without it, the mother’s coldness is inexplicable." Defend or refute with reference to the text’s internal evidence.
questions.a: Refute: the text itself provides sufficient internal evidence — the mother’s "hard little place" in her heart, her expensive tastes, her bitter definition of luck — to explain her coldness as a product of materialist values, not just biography. Biography enriches but is not essential. A wrong answer that agrees uncritically reveals over-reliance on authorial intent at the expense of textual autonomy, a common senior-secondary error.

questions.q: Create a 50-word diary entry dated 1922, written by a fictional middle-class English mother, that captures the same anxiety about "luck" and "style" that haunts Lawrence’s protagonist.
questions.a: A strong entry uses period-appropriate voice (e.g., "Arthur’s prospects vanish like smoke," "the bailiff’s knock," "we wear silk but eat toast") and mirrors the story’s tension between appearance and poverty. A weak entry uses modern slang or generic worry, showing failure to inhabit the historical mindset that the context node builds.
